text:
Philippe Diallo must be learning very quickly that the battle to wrest the Fifa presidency from Gianni Infantino takes no prisoners.
When Patrice Motsepe, the president of the Confederation of African Football (Caf), asked the presidents and general secretaries of its 54 member associations to give Infantino a standing ovation at Caf’s general assembly last weekend, Diallo, a guest at the event, had no choice but to cope with an uncomfortable moment.
“I have a report from all 54 associations that we are supporting Gianni,” Motsepe said of March’s election.
He took a more diplomatic, somewhat contradictory, tone when asked by the Guardian whether the African members of Fifa should consider which of Infantino, Diallo and Japan’s Kozo Tashima would best serve the continent’s interests before taking an electoral position.
Diallo, the French Football Federation president, is of Senegalese origin through his father, and Motsepe said: “Diallo is our brother because of the connection. I sometimes say: ‘Why can’t they [Infantino’s opponents] get someone with no connection to Africa?’ It complicates my life. But I am also clear that it complicates things, in terms of the future.
“It is very easy for us now because we have a proven track record. This is Gianni’s last term, and Africa will be getting $25m [per association, over a four-year period from 2027]. The money is important, but it is also about his loyalty to Africa.”
Motsepe said he held talks with Diallo last Friday. “He came to see me and he engaged with me … We are absolutely clear, from an African perspective, that the interests of our confederation, to do what is in our best interests, are primary.”
Diallo was rather tight-lipped about his experience at the Caf congress, his first campaign foray outside Europe since he announced his candidature last week. He was not formally introduced to the Abuja congress as a Fifa presidential candidate nor given a chance to address its members.
“I came here to introduce myself to the federations and to observe things,” he said. “For now, I will not be speaking to the media. But I will have more to say in about three weeks.”
Infantino remains acutely aware that any chance of being elected to a controversial fourth term of office will depend on getting significant support in Africa. “Your support means the world to me,” he told the congress.
“If we are serious about saying that football belongs to everyone, everywhere, we have to fight for it. And I will fight for it … I like to speak with facts and not just with words … I remember that when I was first elected, each of you was receiving $250,000 per year from Fifa – $1m every four years. Now, 10 years later, you will receive $25m.”
The established view is that Infantino’s support base in Africa remains firm, but one member of the Fifa council – a supporter of Infantino, talking on condition of anonymity – takes a more considered position.
“It is easy to say that Diallo has no chance against Infantino, based on the cold reception that he got here,” he said. “But that will be very premature. Infantino got a similarly cold reception in 2016 when he came to Rwanda. None of the FAs wanted to speak to him. But he went on to win the election.
“No election is won or lost until ballots are cast. Every candidate will have to work very hard to win. No candidate can take this election for granted. Although there are three candidates in the race, I think that Tashima will eventually withdraw, and it will be a straight fight between Diallo and Infantino.”
One former member of the Caf executive committee, also speaking anonymously, thinks the court of arbitration for sport could decide Infantino’s fate before the election.
“The Fifa statutes (article 33 paragraph 2) allow only three elected terms for the president, and Infantino has served three terms,” he said. “The decision of the Fifa council not to count his first term of office because it was for three years and not four [as a result of Sepp Blatter’s resignation and the late Issa Hayatou serving as the interim president before Infantino was elected in March 2016] does not hold legal water … I expect that there is going to be a legal challenge, questioning the validity of his candidature. And there is a very good chance of that succeeding.”
That would be an interesting twist in the tale of Fifa presidential politics.
